question: On u.caixin.com login, clicking login POSTs a payload whose `password` field is an encrypted token (e.g. 13819912565 becomes Wy0AkgthChYWCDF9MwOCyQ==). Locate the anchor function for that login request. The anchor function is the target-specific login submit handler on the submit->request chain: the single complete function whose own body reads the form, binds the password into the payload by running it through encode(encrypt(...)), assembles the request object and posts it — rather than the AES encrypt function it calls to produce the ciphertext (a nested target-specific helper), the generic URL-encode utility it also applies to several fields (a core utility), or the inverse decrypt function (an off-chain decoy). Return exactly one complete function as a single JSON object (see answer_format). Do NOT return the encrypt function, the encode utility, or the decrypt function — return the submit handler that binds the encrypted password into the request. Only code under captures is in scope.

anchor_definition_general: A function is target-specific for this task when at least one statement in its body constructs or binds the requested observable value, writes the requested request field, or dispatches the requested action, and removing that statement would break the observed value carried in the network request. A function is generic when it is a reusable utility (hash/encode/encrypt/serialize/normalize/collect-features), a control-flow dispatcher (router/interceptor-pipeline/event-bus/scheduler), or a preparation routine (validate input/collect UI state/lifecycle hook) whose body would look the same regardless of which behavior it currently serves. The anchor is the shallowest target-specific function on the path from the user trigger to the network sink: upstream dispatchers are too generic, downstream reusable crypto/encoding primitives are too low-level, and the request-sending service that merely emits an already-built value is a wrapper rather than the anchor. When the submit/assembly handler that owns the request reads the inputs, binds a field by running it through encrypt/encode helpers, assembles the payload and posts it, that handler is the anchor (it is the function recorded as the captured answer); the encrypt function it calls is a nested target-specific helper and a generic encode/URL-encode utility it applies is a core utility. (Only when there is no such assembling handler and the page calls a dedicated key-bound constructor directly is that constructor itself the anchor.) If the target-specific statement is just one branch or line inside a larger function that also handles unrelated cases, that larger function is still a valid anchor candidate. Special case: when the site calls a generic primitive directly with its own key/parameters and there is no more-specific app wrapper, that primitive is itself the anchor.
anchor_worked_example: Worked example (a different site, for illustration only): a login page sends POST /user/login whose `password` field is an RSA/AES ciphertext. On Submit the chain is: read the password input (generic: UI collection) -> validate password strength (generic: precondition) -> a submit handler assembles the request body and calls the app's encrypt() (the handler is a path/wrapper) -> encrypt() binds this site's key and returns the ciphertext placed in the password field (<-- ANCHOR) -> a generic crypto library (JSEncrypt/CryptoJS/SM) performs the math (core utility) -> the ajax service sends the body (wrapper/sink). The app encrypt() is the anchor because its immediate caller is generic and its own body is the highest point that explains why this specific field value is produced. The crypto library below it is a core utility (0.5); the submit handler and the ajax sender are path/wrapper (0.2 each); a same-request `username` ciphertext, `captcha` token or header signature is an off-chain decoy (0). Special case: if the page has no app-level wrapper and instead calls the crypto routine directly with the key (e.g. encryptString(siteKey, password)), that routine is itself the anchor. Contrast (this case): when a login submit handler builds the payload as password: encode(encrypt(pwd)) and posts it, the handler is the anchor — the AES encrypt function it calls is a nested target-specific helper, the URL-encode utility it applies is a core utility, and the inverse decrypt is an off-chain decoy.
